## SoundSpotter technology controversy

In 2024, a [WEIRD](https://www.wired.com/story/shotspotter-secret-sensor-locations-leak/) article released internal documents that exposed the locations of a gunshot detection and surveillance tool called ShotSpotter (now renamed "SoundThinking") around Milwaukee, Wisconsin. The ShotSpotter is an audio detection device that can be mounted around the city. Its purpose is to detech gunshot sounds to report to police for investigation. Audio sensors detect loud and explosive sounds that could potentially be gunshots. The algorithm first tries to filter through other confounding sounds like fireworks or cars backfiring, after which the remaining sounds are flagged for a Shotspotter technitian to check once more. The technology was used in Milwaukee since 2010, spending $3.7 million taxpayer money on using and maintaining the technology and signing another $5.25 million contract to continue using the service until March 2026 ([Holmes,2024](
https://wisconsinexaminer.com/2024/02/27/privacy-advocates-respond-to-leaked-data-of-shotspotter-gunshot-detection/ )).

There is no data published on whether or not the ShotSpotter technology improved safety conditions in neighborhoods in Milwaukee since its deployment in 2010. In April 2022, the police department claimed that there was no data available to answer whether the technology improved clearance rate for crimes of police reporting speed, while the homicide rates have fluctuated over time. ([Holmes,2022](https://wisconsinexaminer.com/2022/12/08/is-shotspotter-gunshot-detection-tech-working-for-milwaukee/))


There are multiple layers of data science ethics considerations to this issue, beginning with the choice of location at which the SoundSpotter technology will be mounted at. The company revealed that the criteria for deploying the audio detection devices were based on historic records of gun violence and homicides. The company claims that the "areas that are likely disproportionately impacted by gun violence" are where the devices will mostly be concerntatied in, yet comparisons between the leaked data and the American Community Survey revealed that almost the neighborhoods with at least one SoundSpotter sensor had nearly 70% of the population identifying as Black or Latine. The ethical issue stems further when conclusions about crime, homicides, and safety are drawn from the data gathered over time using the ShotSpotter technology. Might the already disproportionately implemented technology exacerbate the thought that the neighborhoods with high Black or Latine populations are unsafe, and potentially inaccurately draw conclusions between a certain race and crime rates? From another perspective, there is also a meta-level concern about the illegal leakage of the "high-level ShotSpotter sensor locations for several jurisdictions,"  and what implications there might be if exact locations of the sensors are revealed ([Holmes,2024](
https://wisconsinexaminer.com/2024/02/27/privacy-advocates-respond-to-leaked-data-of-shotspotter-gunshot-detection/ )).
